title: Tabernanthe iboga (botany)

source.dataset: psychonautwiki_db.zip (psychonautwiki.db, SQLite export provided by Hany, file dated 2026-11-25)

plain_text:
Tabernanthe iboga, or simply iboga, is a perennial rainforest shrub and psychedelic which is native to western Central Africa. In parts of Africa where the plant grows, the bark of the root is chewed for various pharmacological or ritualistic purposes. Ibogaine, the active alkaloid, is also used to treat substance abuse disorders and depression. A small amount of ibogaine, along with precursors of ibogaine, are found in Voacanga africana.

History

The ibogaine chemical was first isolated by Messrs. J. Dybowski and M. Henri Moissan in 1901.

Descriptions and habitat

It is a small, evergreen, bushy shrub that is found in Gabon, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the Republic of Congo. The yellow root of the plant is the hallucinogen. It has a reputation for being a powerful stimulant and aphrodisiac, and hunters use it to keep themselves awake.

Chemicals

*Ibogaine (C20H26N2O)

Traditional uses

The yellowish root of the plant, which is the hallucinogen, is used in rites of initiation to a number of secret societies to cause a near-death experience as a catalyst for spiritual discovery, including the Bwiti society. Entrance into these societies is conditional on having seen the god plant Bwiti, which is accomplished through the use of iboga. Large doses of iboga induce visions, and sorcerers often use the drug to seek information from their ancestors, as well as the spirit world.
